los.text: Describe the course of the ascending aorta, the arch of the aorta and the descending thoracic aorta, naming the major branches of each division
los.html:
PartCourseBranches
Ascending aortaFrom the aortic valve (behind the left half of the sternum, level of the 3rd costal cartilage) up and right, inside the pericardium, to the sternal angleRight and left coronary arteries (from the aortic sinuses)
Arch
  • Arches back and to the left over the left main bronchus and pulmonary bifurcation
  • Begins and ends at the sternal angle (T4/5)
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian; ligamentum arteriosum attaches underneath (left RLN hooks round it)
Descending thoracicFrom T4/5 down the left of the vertebral bodies, moving to the midline, through the aortic hiatus at T12Posterior intercostal arteries (3rd–11th), subcostal, bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial, mediastinal, superior phrenic
  • Clinical: aortic dissection (tearing pain through to the back), coarctation (just after the left subclavian: rib notching, radiofemoral delay), aneurysm compressing the left RLN (hoarseness).

los.text: Describe the origins, courses and main branches of the left and right coronary arteries and discuss the functional consequences of their obstruction
los.html:
ArteryOrigin and courseMain branchesSupplies
Right coronary (RCA)Right aortic sinus → right atrioventricular groove → round the inferior border → back of the heartSA nodal (~60%), right marginal, AV nodal (~80%), posterior descending (interventricular) in right-dominant heartsRight atrium and ventricle, inferior wall of LV, posterior septum, SA and AV nodes
Left main stemLeft aortic sinus → behind the pulmonary trunk; shortSplits into LAD and circumflex
LAD (anterior interventricular)Down the anterior interventricular groove to the apexDiagonal branches, septal perforatorsAnterior wall of LV, anterior 2/3 of the septum, apex; bundle branches
CircumflexLeft atrioventricular groove round to the backObtuse marginal branches; PDA in left-dominant heartsLateral and posterior LV, left atrium
  • Dominance: whichever artery gives the posterior descending artery (right-dominant in ~70%).
Blocked arteryInfarctECG leadsTypical problems
LAD ("widow-maker")Anterior / anteroseptalV1–V4Large LV loss → heart failure, cardiogenic shock; bundle branch block
CircumflexLateralI, aVL, V5–6Mitral regurgitation (papillary muscle)
RCAInferior (+ right ventricle)II, III, aVFBradycardia and heart block (AV node), RV infarct → hypotension (avoid nitrates)
  • Coronary filling happens mainly in diastole (LV muscle squeezes vessels in systole), so tachycardia reduces supply.

los.text: Explain the venous drainage of the heart
los.html:
VeinRuns withDrains into
Great cardiac veinLAD, then the circumflex in the left AV grooveCoronary sinus
Middle cardiac veinPosterior descending arteryCoronary sinus
Small cardiac veinRight marginal artery, right AV grooveCoronary sinus
Posterior vein of LV, oblique vein of LABack of LV / LACoronary sinus
Anterior cardiac veinsOver the RVDirectly into the right atrium
Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian)In the wallDirectly into all chambers
  • Coronary sinus: in the posterior AV groove
    • opens into the right atrium between the IVC opening and the tricuspid valve.
    • Used for pacing leads (cardiac resynchronisation).

• Anastomosis: a connection between two blood vessels (arteries, veins, or artery to vein) so that blood can reach a region by more than one route.
TypeExample
Arterial (collateral)Circle of Willis, palmar arches, scapular anastomosis, genicular anastomosis
Potential (small, opens slowly)Coronary arteries: functional end arteries, so sudden blockage causes infarction; slow narrowing can grow collaterals
PortosystemicLower oesophagus, rectum, umbilicus (varices in portal hypertension)
ArteriovenousSkin (temperature), surgical AV fistula for dialysis
End arteries (none)Central artery of retina, renal and splenic segmental arteries

los.text: Describe the functions of the pericardium
los.html:
• Fixes the heart in the mediastinum (attached to the diaphragm's central tendon and the back of the sternum).
  • Prevents over-distension of the heart (tough fibrous layer).
  • Lubricates: serous fluid (~20–50 mL) lets the heart beat with little friction.
  • Barrier against infection and spread of disease from the lungs and mediastinum.

los.text: Describe the layout of the pericardium (in relation to cardiac tamponade) and its sinuses
los.html:
LayerDetail
Fibrous pericardiumTough, non-stretch outer sac; fused to the central tendon of the diaphragm and the great vessels' adventitia
Parietal serousLines the fibrous pericardium
Pericardial cavityPotential space with a thin film of fluid
Visceral serous (epicardium)On the heart surface; reflects onto the parietal layer around the great vessels
Transverse sinus
  • Passage behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC and pulmonary veins.
  • Surgeons pass a finger or clamp through it to clamp the great arteries in bypass surgery.
Oblique sinusBlind pocket behind the left atrium, bounded by the pulmonary veins and IVC.
Cardiac tamponade
  • Fluid or blood fills the cavity
  • Because the fibrous layer can't stretch, a small rapid volume (~100–200 mL) squeezes the heart and stops filling.
  • Beck's triad: low BP, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds
  • Pulsus paradoxus.
  • Treat with pericardiocentesis (needle from the left xiphocostal angle, aiming towards the left shoulder).
Slow effusionThe sac can stretch to hold litres before tamponade.

los.text: Explain the concept of pericardial sac and potential space
los.html:
Pericardial sacThe fibrous pericardium + parietal serous layer, enclosing the heart like a fist pushed into a balloon (visceral layer on the heart, parietal layer outside).
Potential space
  • The pericardial cavity normally holds only a film of fluid
  • The layers touch.
  • It becomes a real space only when fluid, blood, pus or air collects (effusion, haemopericardium, purulent pericarditis, pneumopericardium).
Same idea elsewherePleural and peritoneal cavities.

los.text: Recall that the phrenic nerves supply sensation from the pericardium
los.html:
Fibrous pericardium and parietal serous layerSupplied by the phrenic nerves (C3–5), so they feel sharp, localised pain.
Visceral layer (epicardium)Autonomic supply only; insensitive to pain.
CourseBoth phrenic nerves run down in front of the lung roots, between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura (pericardiacophrenic vessels with them), to the diaphragm.

los.text: Explain that pain from the pericardium (pericarditis) may be referred to the shoulder tip because of the common innervation (C3, 4, 5)
los.html:
Pericarditis pain
  • Sharp, central, worse lying flat and breathing in, eased by sitting forward
  • Can spread to the shoulder tip / trapezius ridge.
Why the shoulderThe phrenic nerve's sensory fibres enter the cord at C3–5, the same segments as the supraclavicular nerves (C3–4) supplying shoulder skin, so the brain maps the pain there (referred pain).
Distinguish from MIMI pain is visceral (cardiac sympathetic T1–4: chest, left arm, jaw) and not affected by position.
Other phrenic referralSubphrenic abscess, splenic rupture (Kehr's sign), diaphragmatic pleurisy.
